newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-U.S. ATHLETES DIVIDED ON WORLD MEET WILD CARDS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-U.S. ATHLETES DIVIDED ON WORLD MEET WILD CARDS.

text.p: Competitors at the U.S. athletics championships Thursday were divided over whether American rules should be changed to allow injured stars to compete at the world championships as wild card entries.
World 400-meter record-holder Butch Reynolds doesn't think qualifying rules should be altered to benefit sidelined marquee athletes such as Michael Johnson and decathlete Dan O'Brien.
Olympic hurdles champion Allen Johnson believes the sport's greatest performers should get a chance to make up for missing the lone American qualifying event for the world championships.
The debate arose on a day when U.S. officials passed the buck on wild card entries for the world championships to the International Athletic Federation (IAAF).

"I don't think you should change the sport right now for those two people and create a stigma for them," said Reynolds after running 45.06 seconds, the fastest time in the 400-meter preliminaries at the U.S. championships.

That's exactly what USA Track and Field's executive committee decided Thursday, declining to change the most stringent qualifying procedure in the world in which only the top three finishers in the U.S. championships qualify for the worlds.

But the U.S. federation said if the IAAF wanted to invite world champions to defend their titles in Athens, it would support the decision. That would put double world and Olympic champion Michael Johnson, decathlon world record-holder O'Brien and injured women's sprinter Gwen Torrence in the world championships.
Allen Johnson, who is not related to Michael, thinks that a good idea, to a point.

"If an individual has demonstrated over time that he is head and shoulders above everybody else in the entire world and the world championships doesn't include them, it doesn't make a lot of sense," said the world and Olympic 110-meter hurdles champion. "But we have to be very careful."
For example, Johnson said, the third-place finisher in the U.S. championships should not be excluded from the team to give someone a wild card berth.
Emerging 400-meter runner Milton Campbell agreed with Allen Johnson.
"Michael is the defending world champion," said Campbell. "I say give him a shot. If it is going to knock someone out here, no. But otherwise, I say go for it."
But other 400-meter runners would not change the rule, especially in mid-season.
"I don't really agree with wild cards," Derek Mills said. "My goal this year is to be the world champion, and to have the gold stripped away in any way would hurt."
Jason Rouser also would make no exceptions, despite the fact that many other nations reserve team places for their elite athletes for the Olympics and world championships.
"Michael Johnson is a great athlete, we already know that, but I don't feel that Michael Johnson or any other athlete should be an exception," Rouser said.

"This has been our standards for quite some time, having to go through rounds to make the USA team. This would be an unjust deal to those who didn't make the team in the past for some unusual circumstances."
